A home green to go with ChampionsGate's two championship courses

A backyard putting green in ChampionsGate runs $14–$30 per sq ft installed as of September 2026. Living beside the Omni resort's National and International courses, some homeowners want a home green to work on a stroke between rounds rather than to replace the course itself, and a golf-community lot often backs a lake that sets the buildable area before the design ever starts.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Say you have a 350 sq ft green

Say you have a 350 sq ft green planned for a Stoneybrook South backyard that backs a lake along the National Course, with two tiers and three cups. At $14–$30 per sq ft, that prices between $4,900 and $10,500 depending on fringe turf, cup count and how much shaping the tiers need. Because the lot backs open water, the buildable footprint stops ten feet from the shoreline, which on a typical resort-style lot here still leaves enough room for a green this size closer to the house. The village ARC packet for a green usually wants the same site plan a lawn conversion needs, plus a rough sketch of the contours, since the association is approving a shape as much as a material.

A practice green next to two championship courses, not instead of one

The two Greg Norman designs at Omni Orlando Resort at ChampionsGate, the National Course through former citrus groves and wetlands and the harder International Course built as an inland-links layout, give ChampionsGate residents a reason to want a green at home for something a round on either course doesn't offer: unlimited reps on one specific putt with no group waiting behind. A three- or four-cup home green sized for that kind of practice looks nothing like a course green and doesn't need to; it needs consistent roll on the breaks a homeowner actually plays. A broader look at putting green pricing across Florida and the full putting green guide cover design options beyond what's local to this community.

Cups: the hardware inside a green's design

Cups are cored directly through the finished base at whatever locations the break design calls for, then set and edged so they sit flush with the surrounding putting surface on a ChampionsGate green. The number and placement of cups is as much a product decision as the turf fiber itself, since each one interrupts the shaped surface and has to be positioned where the breaks actually make sense to putt toward. Adding cups after the surface is already down means recutting finished turf, which is why cup locations get fixed during the design phase rather than adjusted later.

Golf-course pond lots decide the buildable footprint first

A lot backing a lake along either course, or a retention pond tucked between fairways, has to keep the green at least ten feet from the water's ordinary line unless a seawall separates the two, and that setback often lands right where a homeowner first imagined the green sitting for the best view of the course beyond it. We confirm the actual water line against the property survey before any shaping design gets drawn, because a green pushed a few feet closer to the view than the setback allows is a green that gets rejected before it gets built.

Why a contoured green still needs an overall slope

Even with tiers and breaks built into the surface for play, a ChampionsGate putting green's base still carries the same one to two percent overall grade toward a drainage point that any lawn does, so the two jobs, holding a shape and shedding water, happen at once rather than one after the other. A green shaped purely for interesting breaks without that underlying slope will hold water in its lowest tier after every storm, regardless of how well the ball rolls the rest of the time. Getting both requirements satisfied in the same base is what separates a green built by someone experienced with the shaping from a flat pad with decoration on top.

When a base is shaped for looks instead of drainage

A ChampionsGate green built by someone chasing dramatic breaks without matching drainage capacity in the low points will look impressive on a dry day and pond badly after the first real storm, since water collects in exactly the tiers designed to be most visually interesting. Standing water sitting in a low tier softens that part of the base well before the rest of the green shows any wear, and the surface above it stops rolling the way it was designed to soon after, sometimes within a single rainy season. Shaping decisions and drainage planning have to happen together from the start, not as a layer added on top of an afterthought base.

Retrofitting a green into a yard versus building both together

Installing a ChampionsGate green into a yard that already has established lawn turf means cutting out and removing the existing product and its base within the green's footprint before the deeper four- to six-inch excavation can even start, an extra step a new-build project skips entirely when lawn and green go in during the same visit. That removal step adds time to a retrofit that a from-scratch job doesn't carry, even though the shaping, seaming, and cup-setting steps that follow are identical either way. Budgeting for that demolition step separately avoids a retrofit quote looking inflated next to a new-construction one for a similarly sized green.

Checking whether a green's break has drifted after two years

By a ChampionsGate green's second year, infill settling and two full rainy seasons of rinsing can shift a break slightly from what it played like on day one, even on a green that was shaped and built correctly. A second-year check means rolling a few balls from the same marked spots used at handoff and comparing the result, since a break that's drifted noticeably usually needs a professional regroom or an infill top-up rather than a full rebuild. Catching this at the two-year mark, rather than waiting until the difference is obvious to every guest who plays it, keeps the fix small.

Someone asking who builds the best putting green near ChampionsGate usually means this

Most calls about a green here aren't about finding a lower price; they're about finding an installer who's shaped a contoured base before; a green built by someone chasing a flat lawn's compaction method instead of a shaped, tiered one tends to hold water in its lowest tier after the first real storm. Ask to see how a prospective installer handles a green's deeper excavation and hand-shaped lifts, since that's the part of the job a lawn quote and a green quote genuinely diverge on, well before the surface product gets chosen.

Questions people ask

Do I need a bigger setback for a green near the golf course than for one anywhere else?

The ten-foot waterbody rule applies to any pond or lake edge the same way, golf-course-adjacent or not, unless a seawall separates the lot from the water. What changes near a course is how often that water shows up on the property line.

Can a putting green go in a ChampionsGate rental villa's backyard?

It can, and a well-built one can be a selling point in a listing description, though the tight lots in some rental sections leave less room for real contouring than a larger gated-village yard does.

Does the state's turf rule change what infill goes in a green here?

Yes, the same as any other lawn: infill on a single-family lot has to be silica sand, rock, shell or another natural material, or coated sand with a non-toxic coating, which covers what most greens already use for roll consistency.
